text:
[FPMC](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/classes/fa17/cse291-b/reading/p811.pdf) adds a user–candidate matrix-factorization score for long-term taste to a previous-item–candidate transition score; basket inputs aggregate previous-basket items. [FOSSIL](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.09152) replaces the explicit user vector with a normalized sum of historical item embeddings, combining this FISM-style preference representation with a weighted sum over the last L items. Lag weights have global and user-specific components. Thus, combining historical preferences with recent embedding signals is established prior art; FOSSIL’s lag weighting captures position without a contextual sequence encoder.

[SASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781) uses causal self-attention, positional embeddings, and nonlinear blocks to construct a history-dependent representation, scored against candidate embeddings. Long- and short-term signals emerge through learned attention rather than separate additive preference and transition branches. Its reported ablations include removing positional embeddings, self-attention blocks, and embedding sharing. Positional embeddings help more on denser datasets; their removal slightly improves Beauty. Attention concentration on recent items demonstrates recency use, but does not by itself establish sophisticated order reasoning.

Recommended controls, rather than reported findings: compare long-term-only, last-item-only, their additive combination, uniform recent-window pooling, lag-weighted pooling, and full SASRec under matched losses, sampling, dimensions, and tuning budgets. Sweep window length. Shuffle earlier history while preserving the last item and window membership; separately shuffle everything to test dependence on the terminal item. Retrain shuffled-history variants alongside inference perturbations to distinguish learnable order benefits from distribution shift. Removing positional embeddings alone is insufficient: causal masking and the terminal-item query retain structural information. Compare frequency-weighted versus deduplicated pooling to isolate repeated-interest effects. With unseen-item candidates, exact-item repeat recommendation is excluded, while repeated historical interests can still help.
